paper_title: CEPO: A General Framework for Improving Prompt Optimization in Multi-Agent Systems

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Multi-agent systems (MAS) require both effective coordination and specialized task execution. Existing prompt optimization approaches typically couple these functions within agent-specific prompts. We introduce Coordinator-Executor Prompt Optimization (CEPO), a general framework for improving prompt optimization in MAS. CEPO separates system-level coordination from agent-level execution through a shared coordinator prompt and agent-specific executor prompts, and guides their updates according to their respective roles. This structure allows shared coordination rules to be refined consistently across agents while keeping execution instructions separately adjustable. CEPO provides the prompt structure and optimization guidance, while existing prompt optimizers perform the underlying search. Extensive experiments spanning 11 benchmarks across four domains demonstrate that applying CEPO to four existing prompt optimizers consistently improves their performance. Ablations and qualitative analyses support the proposed design, while controlled studies on a document-understanding MAS further demonstrate improved optimization budget efficiency and performance scaling with the number of agents.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in reasoning, tool use, and cross-modal grounding (Achiam et al., 2023; Schick et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2023b), enabling multi-agent systems (MAS) (Wu et al., 2024; Li et al., 2023; Zhuge et al., 2024) in which specialized agents collaborate on complex tasks. These systems have shown promising results across document understanding (Han et al., 2025a; Sun et al., 2025), mathematical reasoning (Du et al., 2024; Yuan & Xie, 2025), code generation (Islam et al., 2024), and video understanding (Liu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026a). However, realizing their potential requires both effective system-level coordination and specialized agent-level execution. In other words, each agent must perform their assigned tasks well while working together toward the systems overall goal. Prompt optimization automates the search for effective instructions and has expanded from singleagent settings (Zhou et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024; Pryzant et al., 2023; Ye et al., 2024) to multi-agent systems (Zhou et al., 2026; Zhuge et al., 2024). Recent methods jointly optimize agent prompts or incorporate feedback from downstream interactions and system-level outcomes (Han et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2026b). However, even when these methods account for agent interactions, their prompt updates typically target only agent-specific prompts, within which system-level coordination and agent-level execution remain coupled. Revising shared coordination rules can therefore require consistent changes across multiple prompts with different execution responsibilities. This raises our central question: how can prompt structure and optimization guidance make existing prompt optimizers more effective for MAS? We introduce Coordinator-Executor Prompt Optimization (CEPO), general framework for improving prompt optimization in multi-agent systems. CEPO specifies how prompts are structured and how their updates are guided, while existing prompt optimizers carry out the underlying search. The framework combines two complementary components. Each agent receives this shared coordinator prompt together with its own executor prompt, which specifies how it performs its assigned task. This structure allows single coordination update to apply consistently across all agents while keeping each agents execution instructions separately adjustable. Second, role-aligned optimization provides distinct meta-instructions that guide coordinator updates toward team-level collaboration and executor updates toward each agents task execution. Together, these components make coordination and execution explicit optimization targets that can be refined using different underlying optimizers. We apply CEPO to four different prompt optimizers (PE2, OPRO, ProTeGi, and MASPO) (Ye et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024; Pryzant et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2026b) and conduct extensive experiments on 11 benchmarks across four domains: document understanding, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and video understanding. Across the evaluated settings, CEPO consistently improves performance over the corresponding optimizers without CEPO, demonstrating its applicability to both general-purpose and MAS-specific prompt optimizers. Beyond these performance gains, controlled studies on MDocAgent show improved optimization budget efficiency and performance scaling with the number of agents. Component ablations, optimization-guidance swaps, and qualitative prompt analyses further support the benefits of separating coordination from execution and aligning optimization guidance with each components role. Our main contributions are as follows. We propose two principles to address the coupling of coordination and execution, common limitation of existing MAS prompt optimization. We decompose prompts into shared coordinator prompt for system-level coordination and agent-specific executor prompts for agent-level execution, and apply role-aligned guidance for each. We integrate these two principles into CEPO, general framework for MAS prompt optimization. Applying CEPO to four different prompt optimizers yields consistent gains in extensive experiments spanning eleven benchmarks across four domains.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Multi-Agent Systems for Complex Reasoning. LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) distribute complex tasks across multiple agents. In document understanding, agents gather multimodal evidence, verify intermediate answers, and synthesize findings (Han et al., 2025a; Sun et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025). Mathematical reasoning systems use debate and iterative reflection to refine candidate solutions (Du et al., 2024; Yuan & Xie, 2025). Code generation systems assign complementary roles for planning, programming, testing, and debugging (Islam et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2023a). Video understanding systems combine multimodal evidence processing, temporal localization, and hypothesis verification through agent collaboration (Kugo et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026a). Across these domains, effective collaboration depends on both system-level coordination and agent-level execution, motivating the study of how prompts supporting these functions should be structured and optimized. Prompt Optimization. Prompt optimization automates the search for effective instructions, from single-agent tasks (Zhou et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024; Pryzant et al., 2023; Ye et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2024) to compound systems (Yuksekgonul et al., 2025; Khattab et al., 2024; Opsahl-Ong et al., 2024). Recent work extends optimization to MAS through joint search over prompts and topology (Zhou et al., 2026; Zhuge et al., 2024) and collaborative optimization of agent prompts (Han et al., 2025b; Zhang et al., 2026; Hong et al., 2026). MASPO (Wang et al., 2026b) further incorporates downstream interactions and coordination failures into prompt optimization. Although these approaches account for dependencies among agents, they typically do not explicitly separate system-level coordination and agent-level execution into distinct prompt components, nor provide role-aligned optimization guidance. To address this gap, we propose Coordinator-Executor Prompt Optimization (CEPO), framework that introduces shared coordinator prompt and agent-specific executor prompts and optimizes each according to its role, which complements the underlying prompt optimizer.

sections.title: 3 METHOD
sections.content: We propose Coordinator-Executor Prompt Optimization (CEPO), general framework for improving existing prompt optimizers in multi-agent systems. CEPO combines two components: coordinatorexecutor prompt decomposition, which separates shared coordination from agent-specific execution, and role-aligned optimization, which guides updates to each component according to its function. We first formulate the MAS prompt optimization problem (3.1), then introduce the two design principles and their implementation (3.2), and finally describe the optimization procedure (3.3).

Updating pC changes the shared instructions received by all agents, whereas updating p(i) changes the local instructions of agent Ai. Principle 2: Role-aligned optimization. To ensure that the coordinator and executor prompts are optimized for their intended roles, we propose role-aligned optimization. We implement this strategy using role-specific optimization meta-instructions, ΦC and ΦE, which are supplied to the underlying optimizer. When updating pC, ΦC directs the optimizer to refine system-level collaboration, including cross-agent communication, handling of conflicting evidence, and shared reasoning norms. When updating p(i) , ΦE directs it to refine the target agents execution, including task scoping, evidence use, and concrete procedures under the shared coordination context. Thus, ΦC provides system-level guidance on how agents should coordinate, whereas ΦE provides agent-level guidance on how each agent should execute its assigned task. Note that both prompt layers are selected according to the system-level performance objective J. The meta-instructions provide different guidance for their updates, although they do not define separate numerical objectives. sections.title: IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
sections.content: Benchmarks and evaluation. We evaluate CEPO on eleven benchmarks across four domains: document understanding (MMLongBench-Doc (Ma et al., 2024), LongDocURL (Deng et al., 2025), and PaperTab, PaperText, and FetaTab (Hui et al., 2024)), mathematical reasoning (AQuA (Ling et al., 2017), MATH-500 (Lightman et al., 2024), and AGIEval-MATH (Zhong et al., 2024)), code generation (HumanEval-ET (Dong et al., 2025) and MBPP (Austin et al., 2021)), and video understanding (LongTVQA+ (Liu et al., 2026)). Since the document benchmarks lack dedicated training sets, we partition their test sets into documentlevel train/validation/test splits of 10/10/80 using fixed seed. Baseline scores on our test splits are close to those on the original test sets (Appendix A.1). We evaluate answers with GPT-5mini following the LLM-as-judge protocol of (Han et al., 2025a) (Appendix C.1). We follow MASPO (Wang et al., 2026b) for mathematical reasoning and code generation settings. For video understanding, we follow LongVideoAgent (Liu et al., 2026), retaining its test set and reserving 50 questions from its training set for validation. Underlying prompt optimizers. For document experiments, we use PE2 (Ye et al., 2024) with GPT-5.4 as the optimizer LLM and TC = TE = 3. We also evaluate ProTeGi (Pryzant et al., 2023) and OPRO (Yang et al., 2024) on MDocAgent across all five benchmarks with the same LLM and iteration budgets, retaining each optimizers default hyperparameters  (Table 8)  . For mathematical reasoning and code generation, we follow the official MASPO (Wang et al., 2026b) configurations. With MASPO, CEPO first optimizes the coordinator for up to TC = 4 rounds. Then, with the coordinator fixed, we perform two Predictor updates followed by two Reflector updates and repeat this sequence twice (TE = 4 per executor). GPT-5-mini generates and evaluates prompt candidates. For video understanding, we use PE2 with GPT-5.4 and TC = TE = 3, optimizing the coordinator first and then optimizing the grounding agents executor prompt.

sections.title: 4.2 RESULTS
sections.content: Document understanding. Table 2 presents the results of applying PE2 + CEPO to MDocAgent and DocAgent across five document benchmarks. Compared to their unoptimized baselines, both systems improve on every benchmark, with average gains of 4.3 and 2.7 points, respectively. The largest gain occurs on MMLongBench-Doc with DocAgent, where the score rises from 59.5 to 67.4 (+7.9 points). These consistent gains across both agent systems and all five benchmarks demonstrate that the benefits extend across diverse document understanding tasks. Mathematical reasoning and code generation. Table 3 evaluates CEPO with MASPO (Wang et al., 2026b) on mathematical reasoning and code generation. MASPO + CEPO outperforms both the baseline and MASPO alone on all five benchmarks, achieving an average gain of 5.07 points over the baseline. These results show that explicit coordinator-executor decomposition and role-aligned optimization can complement prompt optimizer that is already tailored to multi-agent systems. Long video understanding. Table 7 shows that applying CEPO on top of PE2 further improves LongVideoAgent (Liu et al., 2026) on LongTVQA+ to 64.9, yielding gain of 1.5 points over vanilla PE2 and 4.6 points over baseline, demonstrating that CEPO is effective for long-video understanding. sections.title: 4.3 ANALYSIS
sections.content: Unless otherwise stated, the following analyses use PE2 with MDocAgent on MMLongBench-Doc. MDocAgent supports controlled changes to agent configurations and optimization targets, while MMLongBench-Doc includes diverse document reasoning cases. CEPO improves optimization budget efficiency. Table 5 shows that PE2 + CEPO with TC = TE = 1 reaches 60.1, exceeding vanilla PE2 with three executor iterations by 2.2 points while using fewer optimizer and MAS API calls. At comparable API-call budgets, PE2 + CEPO with TC = TE = 3 reaches 61.0, whereas vanilla PE2 with six executor iterations reaches 57.4. Additional controls examine inference cost (Table S5) and prompt length (Table S8): CEPO incurs little inference overhead in this document setting, and extending vanilla PE2s prompts to comparable length does not recover CEPOs performance. These results support the value of how prompts are structured and optimized beyond simply increasing the optimization budget or prompt length. CEPO improves performance scaling with MAS size. Figure 3 compares the unoptimized system, vanilla PE2, and PE2 + CEPO on MDocAgent configurations containing one to five agents. The unoptimized system gains little as agents are added, while vanilla PE2 exhibits non-monotonic trend and falls below the unoptimized result at three agents. PE2 + CEPO shows monotonic increase in the reported scores, reaching 61.0 at five agents, and its advantage over the unoptimized system grows from 3.9 points at two agents to 6.9 at five agents. With two agents, it already exceeds the best unoptimized five-agent result. These observations support the benefit of explicit coordination optimization as the number of collaborating agents increases in this system. The executor specifies how to combine OCR and image evidence, ground answers, and extract table information. These examples illustrate the distinction between shared coordination and agent-specific execution under role-aligned guidance.

sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We presented CEPO, general framework that addresses shared limitation in MAS prompt optimization: coupled coordination and execution. By combining coordinator-executor prompt decomposition with role-aligned optimization, CEPO enables existing optimizers to refine both components considering their respective roles. Applying CEPO to four different prompt optimizers yields consistent gains in extensive experiments spanning eleven benchmarks across four domains. Controlled studies further support the proposed design and show improved optimization budget efficiency and performance scaling with MAS size.

sections.title: AI USE STATEMENT
sections.content: LLMs are used as components of our experimental framework, including prompt optimization and LLM-as-judge evaluation, as described in the paper. We also used generative AI tools to assist with coding during experiments, to identify and retrieve relevant literature, and to improve the clarity and language of the manuscript. The authors take responsibility for the final manuscript, code, analyses, and reported results.

sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: CEPO can reduce the manual effort required to design prompts for multi-agent systems, making these systems more accessible. However, easier prompt optimization may encourage deployment without sufficient validation. Optimized prompts can still produce unintended model behavior, particularly in high-stakes or out-of-distribution settings. We therefore recommend task-specific validation and appropriate human oversight before deployment.

sections.title: REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT
sections.content: Section 3 presents CEPO and its optimization procedure. Section 4.1 and Appendix describe the experimental setup, dataset splits, model configurations, and computing resources. Appendix provides evaluator prompts, optimization meta-instructions, and examples of initial and optimized prompts. We plan to release the full codebase upon acceptance.

sections.title: A EXPERIMENTAL DETAILS
sections.content: A.1 DATASET STATISTICS We split each dataset at the document level with 10/10/80 train/validation/test ratio: documents are randomly shuffled and assigned to splits, and all questions associated with given document are kept together. Since many documents contain multiple questions (Table S2), question-level split would leak shared document context across splits. As shown in Table S1, performance on our custom test split closely matches that on the original test split, confirming that our split does not introduce an easier evaluation. For mathematical reasoning and code generation, we use the same datasets and splits as MASPO (Wang et al., 2026b). For LongTVQA+, we use the same test set as LongVideoAgent (Liu et al., 2026). We hold out 50 questions from the original training set for validation and use the remainder as our training set. A.2 COMPUTING RESOURCE For MDocAgent, the agent backbone is Qwen-3.5 (4B) (Qwen Team, 2026), served locally on 8H200 GPUs. For DocAgent, the agent backbone is GPT-5-mini, accessed through the OpenAI API. For the video experiments, we use Qwen2.5-7B as the locally served master agent, while the grounding and vision agents are powered by GPT-5-mini through the OpenAI API. We use GPT-5.4 as the optimizer LLM. A.3 FURTHER IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS We instantiate CEPO on two competitive multi-agent systems for document understanding. MDocAgent (Han et al., 2025a) is five-agent multi-agent system (GENERAL, CRITIC, TEXT, IMAGE, SUM) that splits processing across text and image modalities: the GENERAL and CRITIC agents produce initial answer and identifies crucial clues, the TEXT and IMAGE agents process modalityspecific evidence, and the SUM agent aggregates all intermediate outputs into the final answer. DocAgent (Sun et al., 2025) is three-agent actor-reviewer-reflector. The actor drafts an answer, the reviewer critiques it, and the reflector revises the answer based on the critique. Agents in MDocAgent and DocAgent are powered by Qwen-3.5 (4B) (Qwen Team, 2026) and GPT-5-mini, respectively. Executor prompts are initialized from the default prompts published with each system, and the coordinator prompt for CEPO is initialized by querying GPT-5-mini with brief description of the agent composition (Appendix C.4). A.4 CONFIGURATION BY NUMBER OF AGENTS Table S3 reports the per-configuration breakdown underlying the agent-count analysis in the main text. From the full set of 5 agent roles (GENERAL, CRITIC, TEXT, IMAGE, SUM), we construct subsets of size 1 to 5 and retain only those configurations that produce valid final answer. When multiple valid configurations exist for given agent count, we report each configurations accuracy individually and provide the arithmetic mean across them as the headline result; the bold row in each group indicates the value used for cross-group comparison. We compare three settings: baseline (unoptimized prompts), PE2, and PE2 + CEPO. Across all agent counts and individual configurations, CEPO consistently outperforms both baseline and vanilla PE2, with the margin over baseline growing from 3.9 at 2 agents to 6.9 at 5 agents. Vanilla PE2 is less stable, even falling slightly below baseline at 3 agents due to sharp drop on GENERAL + TEXT + SUM.

sections.title: B FURTHER ANALYSIS
sections.content: B.1 COST ANALYSIS Optimization cost comparison. Table S4 examines accuracy as we vary the optimization budget (TC, TE). We adopt PE2s default iteration budget for each phase of (TC=3, TE=3) for CEPO, which matches the empirical plateau: pushing the budget further to (TC=4, TE=4) yields no improvement and in fact degrades accuracy from 61.0 to 58.6. When matched against PE2 under comparable budgets, CEPOs gains do not stem from spending more compute. CEPO with (TC=1, TE=1) already improves over PE2 with (TC=0, TE=3) by 2.2 points (60.1 vs. 57.9) while using far fewer API calls, showing that even minimal optimization budget yields substantial benefit. At nearidentical optimization cost to PE2 with (TC=0, TE=6), CEPO with (TC=3, TE=3) still leads by 3.6 points (61.0 vs. 57.4), confirming that the advantage comes from more effective optimization rather than from an inflated budget. Inference cost comparison. Table S5 reports the inference cost of each method, measured as average wall-clock time per sample. Since input text tokens are dominated by image tokens in the MDocAgent pipeline, throughput is driven primarily by intermediate output length rather than by prompt length. CEPO produces intermediate outputs comparable in length to the baseline (PE2 + CEPO: 824.7 vs. baseline: 847.7 tokens) yet improves accuracy by 6.9 points, while vanilla PE2 reaches lower accuracy (57.9) with shorter intermediates (595.8 tokens). This indicates that prompts optimized with CEPO elicit richer intermediate reasoning at no additional inference cost compared to the baseline, whereas vanilla PE2s compactness comes at an accuracy cost.

Table S6 ablates the optimization schedule along two axes: schedule type (sequential vs. alternating) and starting role (coordinator-first vs. executor-first). Here, alternating schedule denotes optimizing each agent in turn for single iteration. Sequential schedules outperform alternating ones, as letting each role converge before switching avoids the instability of co-adapting two interdependent prompts. Optimizing the coordinator first is also preferable, since fixing the high-level pipeline behavior early provides stable target against which the executors can specialize. Our choice combines both, yielding the highest accuracy of 61.0. Analysis on target executor set I. Table S7 ablates the choice of the target executor set I, the set of agents whose executor prompts are optimized. For = 1, we report results for every agent individually.
